title: Trending — People prefer to negotiate with women, even when outcomes are identical and gender is unknown
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
one_line: Across MBA-classroom and anonymous online negotiations with over 2,000 participants, counterparts reported higher subjective value (trust, rapport, desire to negotiate again) with women while economic outcomes were identical.
key_claims: In archival face-to-face MBA negotiation data (>2,000 observations, 230+ students), women generated significantly higher subjective value with no difference in distributive or integrative economic outcomes.
The preference persisted in anonymous text-chat negotiations (>1,000 dyads, paid $0.83/point) where third-party observers guessed negotiator gender correctly only 43% of the time — worse than chance.

An NLP model (Vanderbilt AI negotiation lab, 12 behavioral codes) found women more likely to make multi-issue offers and accept offers, while men more often provided information; serial mediation linked these behaviors to subjective value without economic cost.

Observers rated women higher on both warmth and competence, contradicting the stereotype content model's assumed trade-off; preference for women counterparts held even in competitive zero-sum negotiations (13-item subjective value inventory, Study 4).

A Monte Carlo simulation using observed re-engagement rates (94.4% for women vs 91.9% for men) projected women accumulating ~44–56% more negotiation opportunities, e.g. ~$178,000 over ~18 negotiations vs ~$123,000 over ~12 for men.
limitations: Authors note all studies used low-ambiguity settings where negotiating was explicitly sanctioned; prior work (Bowles et al. 2005) shows women penalised when appropriateness of negotiating is ambiguous.
Career earnings gap is a simulation, not observed longitudinal data.
Settings are MBA coursework and an online resource-allocation game, not real workplace negotiations.
Behavioral coding depends on an AI classifier's 12-category scheme, which may miss other mechanisms.
Risk of 'unmitigated communion' (relationship concern destroying economic value) was avoided here but not tested across contexts.
open_questions: Does the subjective-value advantage survive in high-ambiguity, real-stakes workplace negotiations where women face documented penalties?
Would randomly assigning the identified behaviors (multi-issue offers, strategic acceptance) to men reproduce the subjective-value gain, proving behavior rather than gender is causal?
Do the simulated compounding opportunity gains appear in actual longitudinal career data?
